title: Feedback Loops: Why Systems Do the Opposite of What You Expect
subtitle: Push on a complex system and it often pushes back — or spirals out of control. Learn to see the loops and the world stops being baffling.
hook: Build a wider highway to cut traffic, and traffic gets *worse*. Crack down hard on a problem, and it sometimes explodes. Complex systems — economies, ecosystems, companies, your own habits — routinely do the opposite of what a straight-line guess predicts. The reason is almost always **feedback loops**: effects that circle back and become causes. See the loops and you gain a kind of X-ray vision for how the world actually behaves.

sections.heading: Two kinds of loop
sections.body:
**Reinforcing loops** amplify: more causes more. Money earning interest earning interest; a viral post getting shares that get more shares; a panic where selling causes more selling. They produce explosive growth or collapse.

**Balancing loops** stabilize: they push back toward a target. A thermostat cutting the heat as the room warms; your body sweating to cool down; prices rising to choke off excess demand. They produce stability — or stubborn resistance to the change you're trying to force.

sections.caption: Reinforcing loops snowball (growth/collapse); balancing loops self-correct toward a target. Most systems are a tangle of both.

sections.label: Why interventions backfire
sections.body: Push on a system and a **balancing loop** may quietly cancel you (wider roads → more people choose to drive → traffic returns: 'induced demand'). Or you trip a **reinforcing loop** and get a runaway you didn't intend. The fix isn't to push harder — it's to find the loop and change its structure. Leverage lives in the loops, not the effort.

sections.label: Delays make it worse
sections.body: Loops often act with a **delay** — the effect shows up long after the cause, so we misread what's happening and overcorrect (think of adjusting a shower with slow-reacting taps: scald, freeze, scald). Delays turn sensible reactions into oscillations. When a system keeps overshooting, suspect a delayed feedback loop.

sections.caption: Reinforcing vs. balancing feedback loops — the heart of systems thinking.

takeaways: Complex systems surprise us because effects **loop back** to become causes.
**Balancing loops** stabilize (thermostats: push back toward a target).
Interventions backfire when a balancing loop cancels them or a reinforcing loop runs away.
**Delays** in loops cause overshoot and oscillation — leverage is in the structure, not brute force.

quiz.q: Money earning interest that itself earns interest is which kind of loop?
quiz.explain: Reinforcing: more leads to more — a snowball (this is compounding again!).

quiz.q: A wider highway leads to MORE traffic. Best explanation?
options: A balancing loop / induced demand — easier driving pulls in more drivers until it re-clogs
quiz.explain: The system pushes back toward its old equilibrium — pushing harder doesn't help; changing structure does.

quiz.q: CALLBACK + BOSS: Which earlier lesson is literally a reinforcing feedback loop in disguise?
options: Compounding / exponential growth (Days 2 & 8) — interest feeds back to earn more interest
quiz.explain: Exponential growth IS a reinforcing loop: the output becomes the next round's input. Compounding, viral spread, and runaway systems are the same shape.

tg_quiz.q: A thermostat cooling a warming room is which loop?
tg_quiz.correct: Right — balancing: it pushes back toward a target.
tg_quiz.wrong: Balancing — it self-corrects toward a set point (unlike a snowball).
